newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea says military to aid harvest.
newsitem.headline: North Korea says military to aid harvest.

text.p: North Korea announced on Sunday that its armed forces were joining an all-out battle against food shortages in the famine-hit communist nation.

In a sign of growing desperation about how to feed people, an official Korean Radio report, monitored in Tokyo, said the armed forces would take on any agricultural task to ensure a "bumper harvest" this year.

North Korean analysts said the announcement could also be an veiled answer to some Western nations' reluctance to give aid to a nation which has managed to keep 1.1 million troops under arms despite its economic plight.

The radio said meetings of commanding officers and soldiers from the army, navy, and air force, communist party officials and people from all walks of life had decided on a war on food shortages caused by two years of record floods.

The meetings agreed that soldiers "must further solidify the unity of the army and people and achieve a bumper harvest this year without fail by launching into the struggle to assist rural areas and actively contribute to agricultural production."
Soldiers would take "a plunge into water or fire for any task to increase grain output for the people," the radio said.
Devastated by floods in 1995 and 1996, North Korea needs at least 1.3 million tonnes of additional food to meet just its basic needs this year, a United Nations food aid agency said recently.
North Korean authorities have said their food supplies were due to run out by the end of April.

Food aid has become a key issue in negotiations to get North Korea to join peace talks with the rival south, the United States and China to formally close the book on the 1950-53 Korean war which ended in an armistice.
North Korea has insisted that it wants far more than already promised humanitarian aid from the United States to start negotiations.
The United States has made clear that once peace talks start, stepped up aid was a strong possibility.
Hong Kong's South China Morning Post reported on Sunday that many North Korean soldiers were starving and roaming famine-hit cities and rural areas with their weapons demanding food and money,

The newspaper, which based its story on reports from ethnic Korean Chinese returning to China after visits to relatives in the impoverished state, said the accounts contradicted Pyongyang claims that it had been able to keep its army under control.

"In Namyang city, soldiers wandered the streets at night. If they saw a light, they would break into homes threatening people with guns, demanding food and money," Kim Chan-shan, 50, was quoted as saying after returning from a three-week visit.
Last month World Food Programme chief Catherine Bertini said food shortages had become so bad that people were eating tree bark and rations to the military had been cut for the first time.
Bertini warned the situation was so dire that North Korea could run out of food by June.
She said North Korea's 23 million people were existing on 100 grams (3-1/2 ounces) of rice a day, half last year's amount, and a quarter of what people received before the two years of flood.
